newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy Treasury says no accounting tricks for EMU.
newsitem.headline: Italy Treasury says no accounting tricks for EMU.

text.p: The Italian Treasury rejected criticism of resorting to creative accounting in order to reach the 3.0 percent deficit/GDP ratio parameter set for early entry into the single European currency.

Financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore on Saturday, referring to the change of status of state railway Ferrovie dello Stato (FS) loans and credits approved by parliament, talked of "a first tranche of creative financing" and "tricks for Europe."
But the Treasury said in a statement on Saturday that no tricks were being used and all balance sheet accounting procedures were in order and being strictly applied.

The lower house of parliament, examining the government's tough 1997 draft budget law article by article, on Friday approved a measure converting FS state loans into a form of direct state debt, so reducing the burden on state accounts.
The measure passed is part of 12.5 trillion lire worth of so-called Treasury operations within the budget which aims to lop 62.5 trillion lire off next year's deficit.

The new measure will allow the conversion of 3.0 trillion lire of transfers to the FS into a form of state equity stake or capital increase in FS, thus reducing the burden on the state deficit by the same amount.
The state will save a further 3.0 trillion lire by also considering funds for programmed FS contracts as a form of capital transfer and no longer as direct state expenditure.

Il Sole said some of the funds the state transferred to the FS now became "below the line" transactions in accounting terms and capital transfers were excluded from public administration accounts, the parameter used by the Maastricht Treaty in its definition for entry into Europe's economic and monetary union.
"Tricks? And why not," Il Sole said, "the battle against the deficit is in large part a real war."

But the Treasury said in its statement that no "accounting artifice" was involved and that measures used were "a correct application of the accounting criteria to calculate public administration net debt, which is one of the Maastricht parameters."
The government's deficit targets set out in its 1997/99 economic plan were based on public sector accounts and not on public administration accounts.
But Treasury officials have said that both the public administration deficit/GDP ratio goal and the public sector deficit/GDP ratio would be around 3.0 percent in 1997.

The Treasury said that in past weeks talks had been held between the state auditor, the Treasury and the European Commission to define the most appropriate accounting criteria to calculate Italy's public administration net debt.

"What has emerged is that certain budget operations, currently being examined by the lower house of parliament, will have the effect of reducing the deficit but not the net debt, and vice versa," the Treasury's statement added.
The lower house has until November 14 to ratify the 1997 budget package which then passes to the upper house Senate. The budget must be approved by December 31.
